problem: Sim-trained visual navigation policies are known to suffer a sim2real gap, and prior work never directly compared sim-trained policies against policies trained on real-world data for the same task. Existing real-data topological navigation policies (ViNT, NoMAD, PlaceNav) also generalize poorly across illumination and cameras.
motivation: Real-world data collection is labor-intensive and platform-specific, while simulation scales cheaply and allows on-policy learning. Knowing whether simulation-only training can match real data determines how robot navigation data should be collected.
key_idea: A lightweight 12M-parameter topological goal-reaching policy built on a frozen distilled multi-teacher pretrained visual encoder (Theia) plus a binocular goal encoder, trained in Habitat with DAgger on 12M samples, matches or beats real-data-trained policies on real robots.
insight: Diverse pretrained encoder features bridge the appearance gap: frozen ImageNet EfficientNet-B0 gets 0.13 real SR versus 0.80 for Theia CDDSV (both DAgger). On-policy learning matters most: BC and DAgger are similar in sim (0.87 vs 0.91) but differ greatly in real (0.23 vs 0.80). Data scale alone is not enough, since Sim BC with 12M samples fails, and real-data BC shows the same spinning failure loops.
method: Frozen PVR: Tiny CDDSV Theia encoder (5M params) distilling CLIP, DINOv2, Depth Anything, SAM and ViT; kept frozen to avoid overfitting and give robustness to appearance shift.

Binocular goal encoder: 4-layer, 4-head transformer decoder, CroCo-inspired, alternating self-attention on goal tokens and cross-attention to observation tokens; learns implicit correspondences end-to-end without supervision.

Sequence encoder: patch tokens compressed by a 2D conv and flattened, non-causal 4-layer/4-head transformer with a learnable state token feeding a predictor head that outputs H=5 SE(2) waypoints from P=6 observations; a PD controller converts them to velocities.

Sim training: imitates a shortest-path oracle with privileged simulator state, subgoals sampled 0.5-3.0 m apart, MSE loss; DAgger with student-action probability beta^r (beta=0.8, 10 rounds) in Habitat on HM3D train, 110° FOV, 224x126 images, color jitter and posterization augmentation.
Real training: BC on RECON, GoStanford, SACSoN, SCAND and TartanDrive (~1.2M frames at 4 Hz), hindsight-relabeled goals, per-dataset waypoint normalization, no temporal distance prediction.
Deployment: PlaceNav framework with an EigenPlaces ResNet18 place recognition subgoal selector plus Bayesian filtering, both threads at 4 Hz onboard a Jetson Orin; topological map images every 5 s.

setting.backbone: FAINT: frozen Theia Tiny CDDSV encoder + trained binocular/sequence transformers (12M params total)
setting.training_data: Sim: 12.0M samples from Habitat HM3D train PointNav routes with DAgger from a shortest-path oracle. Real variant: ~1.2M frames from RECON, GoStanford, SACSoN, SCAND and TartanDrive.
setting.observation: monocular egocentric RGB (history of 6 frames) plus subgoal image, 110° FOV
setting.action_space: predicted SE(2) waypoints (H=5), converted by a PD controller to velocity commands
setting.simulator: Habitat (HM3D) for training; real Turtlebot4 and drone for evaluation
setting.privileged: none at test time (the oracle uses the privileged simulator state only for training labels)

results: Sim-trained FAINT reaches 0.75 total real SR versus 0.44 for the real-data version (+31 points), and 0.90 versus 0.40 for ViNT, the strongest baseline (+50 points). Sim10% (1.2M samples) gets only 0.22, showing scale and on-policy data both matter. The same sim-trained model deployed on a drone without modification navigated open-space routes, though only two were tested and one goal was missed.
limitations: Real-world evaluation is limited to indoor environments, short routes (5-25 m) and small trial counts (e.g. n=48/63), and cross-embodiment drone results are preliminary (two routes).
The real vs sim comparison is confounded by dataset size (1.2M vs 12M) and by BC vs DAgger, so the on-policy explanation is a hypothesis rather than a controlled result.
Real-world success is defined by the place recognition module localizing to the last map node, and the policy is trained on kinematic control with no dynamics.
